sections.title: Introduction

summary.text: Introduces product master data and its role in digital health supply chains (Fig. 1–3), alignment with the WHO Digital Implementation Investment Guide (DIIG, Fig. 4), WHO SMART Guidelines L1–L5 knowledge layers and ANC workflow connections (Fig. 5–6), the Digital Health Supply Chain (DHSC) architecture framework (Fig. 7), handbook methodology, target users across Chapters 1–7, and scenarios for using the handbook.

sections.extract: # Introduction Health products pass through multiple supply chain partners and processes as they move from manufacturers to end-users. For transactions to be seamless, all stakeholders must consistently identify health products using standardized information. For example, if a country’s central warehouse receives a shipment of vaccines with identifiers that do not match its standardized data, manual reconciliation

summary.text: Chapter 1 overview explaining the role of Ministries of Health and National Regulatory Authorities (NRAs) in establishing policies and legislation that mandate manufacturers and distributors to supply standardized product master data.

sections.extract: # 01. Establishing regulatory policies to promote product master data standardization Manufacturers and distributors of health products are the source of truth for product master data. Ensuring that manufacturers and distributors consistently provide product master data in a standardized and uniform format is crucial for enabling interoperability and leveraging automation through barcode scanning. sections.title: Leveraging the WHO-hosted PCMT

summary.text: Chapter 6: Describes the WHO-hosted Product Catalogue Management Tool (PCMT) (available in 2026), its conceptual architecture linking the WHO Global Catalogue with Country Catalogues A and B (Fig. 14), and its user-group/category access permission model (`WHOGroup`, `CAGroup`, `CBGroup`), cross-catalogue associations, and copy rules.

sections.extract: # 06. Leveraging the WHO-hosted PCMT Countries planning to implement a digital tool to manage product master data may consider using the WHO–hosted PCMT as an initial option. This tool can serve as a starting point to manage national health product master data while countries build the necessary technical resources and capacity to implement an in-country–hosted solution. Alternatively, countries may continue using

sections.title: Sharing product master data as a global good

summary.text: Chapter 7: Explains the value of sharing national product master data as a global good with the WHO Global Product Catalogue (accurate information, standardization, reduced redundancy, crisis management, equal access, capacity building) and presents the bidirectional data-sharing model across countries and the WHO-hosted PCMT (Fig. 15).

sections.extract: # 07. Sharing product master data as a global good Sharing health product master data with a global repository—such as the WHO Global Product Catalogue—holds significant value and importance as a global good for several reasons: - **Access to accurate information:** A centralized repository enables health professionals and organizations worldwide to access accurate and up-to-date information on health products. -
